# Whether each surface starts with a config file, pinned to the release
# before the config checks were rebuilt (7437238c), so start behaviour cannot
# drift unnoticed. Read by the terminal UI's start test (dux-tui) and by
# `dux server`'s (dux-web tests).
#
# One case per line: <terminal UI> <dux server> <the whole file, as a JSON
# string>. Each outcome is `start` or `refuse`. An outcome that differs from
# 7437238c on purpose is written `<now>(was:<then>)`, for a reason listed
# here:
#
# - A file that is not TOML (a broken header, a key written twice) stops
#   `dux server` too. 7437238c started it on the defaults, silently, which
#   would serve with no web password at all when the file meant to set one.
# - A `[server]` that is not a table (an array of tables, a value) but holds a
#   web UI password setting (a `password_hash`, or an `auth` table) stops
#   `dux server` too. 7437238c reset `[server]` and started with no password;
#   a `[server]` that is not a table and holds none starts as it did then.
# - A `password_hash` anywhere but the real `[server.auth]` (`[Server.auth]`,
#   `[SERVER.AUTH]`, a quoted `["server.auth"]`, `"auth.password_hash"` under
#   `[server]`, `[ui]`, `[defaults]`) stops both surfaces. 7437238c had no
#   web password and ignored such a key, but the hash is a password the user
#   meant to set, and starting without it would serve with none. As a name
#   the user chose (`[env] password_hash`, a provider or a macro called
#   that, a variable in a project's `env`) it is just a name, and the file
#   starts as it did then. A field INSIDE a provider, a macro or a
#   `[[projects]]` entry is a field of dux's schema, not a name, so a
#   `password_hash` there is misplaced and stops both surfaces.
# - A setting `[server.auth]` has, written directly at the top level or
#   directly under `[server]` (`require = "everywhere"` one level too high),
#   stops both surfaces: none of those names is a setting there, so it can
#   only be a misplaced auth setting, and 7437238c reading it as nothing read
#   a mistake as less protection. So does a table under a longer word for it
#   (`[server.authentication]`, `[server.login]`) holding one. Auth key names
#   are matched lowercased with `-` and `_` taken out, so `password-hash`,
#   `passwordHash` and `minimum-password-length` are the names they look
#   like; a name the user chose (`[env] password-hash`, a provider called
#   that) stays just a name.
# - The same holds in every shape a path can take, judged by one rule over
#   the whole file: an auth setting anywhere but exactly `server` > `auth` >
#   the setting, spelled as dux reads it, stops both surfaces. That covers an
#   array of tables (`[[server.auths]]`, `[[server.auth]]`), an inline array,
#   a differently cased `[Server.auth]` or `[SERVER.auth]`, a quoted key
#   holding dots (`"auth.require"`, `["server.auth"]`), a table nested in
#   `[server.auth]`, a field of a provider and the retired top-level `[auth]`
#   holding an auth setting. The real setting written as dotted keys or an
#   inline table still starts, and the retired `[auth]` holding only its old
#   `username` still starts.
# - A map of user-chosen names written as an array (`[[env]]`,
#   `[[providers]]`, `macros = [{ … }]`, a project's `env` as an array) is no
#   map of names, so an auth setting inside it is a misplaced setting, not a
#   name, and stops `dux server` too (the terminal UI already refused these
#   files on their types). A variable named like one in a project's own
#   `env` table, inside the `[[projects]]` list, is still just a name.
#   A `[projects]` written as a table is no list of projects, so its `env`
#   holds no names either.
# - A plaintext `password` (the setting `dux config set server.auth.password`
#   takes, which dux stores only as its hash) is never read from the file, so
#   it stops both surfaces wherever it is written, `[server.auth]` and the
#   retired `[auth]` included: the user meant to protect the web UI, and
#   7437238c started with no password at all. An `[env]` variable named
#   `password` is still just a variable.
# - A key in a map of user-chosen names is a name only when its value has
#   the shape that map's entries have: a string in `[env]` and a project's
#   `env`, a table in `[providers]` and `[macros]`, a key or a list of keys in
#   `[keys]`. Anything else is no entry of the map, so an auth setting
#   written there (a string `password_hash` or `password` under `[macros]` or
#   `[providers]`, a table under `[env]`, a number under `[keys]`) is a
#   misplaced setting and stops `dux server` too. dux's own documented file
#   ended in `[macros]`, so a password line added at its end landed there,
#   and 7437238c started with no password. A string or a list of strings
#   under `[keys]` is a binding's shape and stays a name.
#
# The cases vary every setting 7437238c had (a valid other value and a value
# of the wrong type), the stock and a custom provider field by field, env,
# macro and key names, the deprecated keys, project records, tables of the
# user's own (near "auth" included), a `[server]` that is not a table, names
# holding dots and spaces, and whole-file oddities. [server.auth] did not
# exist then and is not in it, except as a misplaced password setting.

# Every case above that is TOML with at least one table, written again twice:
# once with each section as an inline table (`server = { port = 4000 }`,
# arrays of tables as inline arrays), once with each section as dotted keys
# at the root (`server.port = 4000`; arrays of tables, which dotted keys
# cannot write, stay as they are). A start reads the file as it is written,
# so the way a section is spelled must change nothing a start decides, except
# for the deliberate auth differences listed at the top, which hold however
# the section is written. Outcomes at 7437238c were recorded on these files.
start start "defaults = { provider = \"x\" }\n"
